q: The central bank buys government bonds from the public. What is the first link in the usual expansionary transmission chain?
correctAnswer: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
distractors: Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.
commonError: Skipping the money-supply and interest-rate links after an open-market purchase.
feedback: A bond purchase adds reserves to the banking system, supports money creation, and tends to lower market interest rates.
options: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.

q: Why can lower interest rates increase aggregate demand in the short run?
correctAnswer: They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
distractors: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.
commonError: Treating monetary policy as a direct change in government spending or product prices.
feedback: Lower borrowing costs encourage investment and some durable consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right.
options: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.

q: Money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged. What happens at the new money-market equilibrium?
correctAnswer: The equilibrium interest rate falls.
distractors: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.
commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
feedback: With money demand fixed, a larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate.
options: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
The equilibrium interest rate falls.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.

q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold most of them as excess reserves. How does this affect the transmission mechanism?
correctAnswer: Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.
distractors: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
commonError: Assuming reserve injections always create the same money and credit expansion.
feedback: When banks hold added reserves rather than lending them, money creation and the downstream spending response are weaker.
options: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.

q: Interest rates fall after an expansionary policy, but firms believe future sales will remain weak. What is the likely result?
correctAnswer: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
distractors: Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.
commonError: Assuming lower rates guarantee a large investment response regardless of expectations.
feedback: Weak expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing costs fall, weakening policy transmission.
options: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.

q: Which sequence correctly traces a contractionary open-market operation through aggregate demand?
correctAnswer: Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
distractors: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
commonError: Reversing the reserve, interest-rate, or spending links in contractionary policy.
feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, contracts money and credit, raises rates, reduces interest-sensitive spending, and lowers aggregate demand.
options: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.

q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
correctAnswer: The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
distractors: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The government-purchases multiplier must be 0.75.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The government-purchases multiplier must be 0.75.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.

q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
correctAnswer: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
distractors: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.

q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
correctAnswer: A lower marginal propensity to save.
distractors: A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.

q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
correctAnswer: $40 billion.
distractors: $10 billion.
$20 billion.
$80 billion.
commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.
options: $10 billion.
$40 billion.
$20 billion.
$80 billion.

q: A fiscal package creates a gross $120 billion increase in aggregate demand, but higher interest rates reduce investment by $25 billion. What is the net shift?
correctAnswer: Aggregate demand rises by $95 billion.
distractors: Aggregate demand rises by $145 billion.
Aggregate demand rises by $25 billion.
Aggregate demand falls by $95 billion.
commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the expansion: $120 billion minus $25 billion equals a $95 billion net increase.
options: Aggregate demand rises by $145 billion.
Aggregate demand rises by $25 billion.
Aggregate demand rises by $95 billion.
Aggregate demand falls by $95 billion.

q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
correctAnswer: Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
distractors: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

q: A country puts unemployed workers and idle factories back to work without gaining new technology. How does this appear on its PPF?
correctAnswer: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
distractors: The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.
commonError: Calling movement to the existing frontier economic growth.
feedback: Using existing resources more fully moves production to the frontier; growth requires the frontier itself to shift outward.
options: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.

q: A technological improvement affects only the production of medical equipment, not food. How does the PPF change?
correctAnswer: The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
distractors: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.
commonError: Treating a one-sector technology gain as an equal shift for both goods.
feedback: A productivity gain limited to one good expands the maximum attainable quantity of that good without changing the other intercept.
options: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.

q: Why is a typical PPF bowed outward from the origin?
correctAnswer: Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.
distractors: All resources are equally productive in every use.
Opportunity cost falls as specialization increases.
The economy is producing inside the frontier.
commonError: Attributing the bowed shape to equal resource adaptability or inefficiency.
feedback: As production shifts, resources increasingly unsuited to the expanding good must be reassigned, raising opportunity cost.
options: All resources are equally productive in every use.
Opportunity cost falls as specialization increases.
Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.
The economy is producing inside the frontier.

q: Moving from bundle A to B gains 5 machines and sacrifices 10 tons of food. Moving from B to C gains another 5 machines and sacrifices 20 tons of food. What does the pattern show?
correctAnswer: The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.
distractors: The opportunity cost of machines falls from 4 to 2 tons per machine.
The opportunity cost remains constant at 3 tons per machine.
Bundle C must lie inside the production possibilities frontier.
commonError: Comparing total sacrifices without converting each move to cost per additional unit.
feedback: The first move costs 10/5 = 2 tons per machine; the second costs 20/5 = 4, showing increasing opportunity cost.
options: The opportunity cost of machines falls from 4 to 2 tons per machine.
The opportunity cost remains constant at 3 tons per machine.
Bundle C must lie inside the production possibilities frontier.
The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.

q: Country A chooses more capital goods and fewer consumer goods today than Country B, with otherwise similar resources. What is the likely long-run implication?
correctAnswer: Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
distractors: Country A must have a lower future PPF because current consumption is smaller.
Country B necessarily grows faster because consumption creates capital automatically.
Neither choice can affect future production possibilities.
commonError: Ignoring the link between current investment and future productive capacity.
feedback: Greater current production of capital goods can expand future capacity, though it requires sacrificing current consumption.
options: Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
Country A must have a lower future PPF because current consumption is smaller.
Country B necessarily grows faster because consumption creates capital automatically.
Neither choice can affect future production possibilities.

q: A disaster destroys equipment used only to produce electric power, while agricultural capacity is unchanged. What happens to the PPF?
correctAnswer: Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
distractors: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.
commonError: Treating a sector-specific loss as an equal inward shift or a movement along the same frontier.
feedback: Losing capacity in one sector reduces the maximum output of that good and rotates the frontier inward on that axis.
options: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.

q: A production point lies inside the PPF. How should it be classified?
correctAnswer: It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
distractors: It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
It is efficient because it uses fewer resources.
It proves the economy has experienced long-run growth.
commonError: Treating an inside point as impossible or fully efficient.
feedback: A point inside the frontier is feasible, but the economy could produce more of at least one good with existing resources.
options: It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
It is efficient because it uses fewer resources.
It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
It proves the economy has experienced long-run growth.

q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
correctAnswer: Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
distractors: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.

q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
correctAnswer: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
distractors: Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.

q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
correctAnswer: It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
distractors: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.

q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
correctAnswer: Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
distractors: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.

q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
correctAnswer: Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
distractors: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
commonError: Assuming two expansionary policies cannot create excessive aggregate demand.
feedback: When both policies push spending upward near capacity, the combined demand increase can create an inflationary gap.
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.

q: The central bank tightens monetary policy while the government enacts fiscal expansion. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
correctAnswer: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
distractors: Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.
commonError: Declaring a definite outcome without comparing the strength of opposing policy impulses.
feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes aggregate demand right, while monetary contraction pushes it left; the net change depends on magnitudes.
options: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.

q: Money supply grows 9 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. Using the growth-rate form of MV = PY, what inflation rate is implied?
correctAnswer: Approximately 4 percent.
distractors: Approximately 2 percent.
Approximately 8 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
commonError: Ignoring velocity growth or adding real-output growth instead of subtracting it.
feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus real-output growth: 9 + (-2) - 3 = 4 percent.
options: Approximately 2 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 8 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.

q: The money supply rises once by 10 percent while velocity and real output remain fixed. What does the quantity theory predict?
correctAnswer: The price level rises once; continued inflation needs continued money growth.
distractors: The inflation rate remains 10 percent every year even if money stops growing.
Real output rises permanently by 10 percent with no price change.
Velocity must fall by 10 percent to preserve the equation.
commonError: Confusing a one-time increase in the price level with a permanently higher inflation rate.
feedback: With velocity and real output fixed, a one-time money increase produces a one-time proportional price-level increase.
options: The inflation rate remains 10 percent every year even if money stops growing.
Real output rises permanently by 10 percent with no price change.
The price level rises once; continued inflation needs continued money growth.
Velocity must fall by 10 percent to preserve the equation.

q: In the equation MV = PY, what does velocity measure?
correctAnswer: The average turnover of money in purchases of final output.
distractors: The percentage rate at which the overall price level changes.
The amount of real output produced by each unit of labor.
The interest rate the central bank pays on reserve balances.
commonError: Confusing velocity with inflation, productivity, or an interest rate.
feedback: Velocity links the money stock to nominal spending by measuring the average turnover of money.
options: The percentage rate at which the overall price level changes.
The amount of real output produced by each unit of labor.
The interest rate the central bank pays on reserve balances.
The average turnover of money in purchases of final output.

q: Money grows 10 percent, real output grows 4 percent, and velocity is stable. What inflation rate is predicted?
correctAnswer: Approximately 6 percent.
distractors: Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
commonError: Failing to subtract real-output growth from money growth.
feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is approximately money growth minus real-output growth: 10 - 4 = 6 percent.
options: Approximately 6 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.

q: If money supply and velocity are unchanged while real output rises, what must happen to the price level in MV = PY?
correctAnswer: The price level falls.
distractors: The price level rises.
The price level stays fixed by definition.
Nominal GDP doubles.
commonError: Assuming higher real output always raises the price level when nominal spending is fixed.
feedback: If MV is unchanged and Y rises, P must fall so that PY continues to equal nominal spending.
options: The price level rises.
The price level falls.
The price level stays fixed by definition.
Nominal GDP doubles.

q: Money supply grows 12 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. What inflation rate follows from the quantity equation?
correctAnswer: Approximately 7 percent.
distractors: Approximately 3 percent.
Approximately 11 percent.
Approximately 17 percent.
commonError: Adding all growth rates or ignoring the decline in velocity.
feedback: Inflation is 12 + (-2) - 3 = 7 percent.
options: Approximately 3 percent.
Approximately 11 percent.
Approximately 7 percent.
Approximately 17 percent.

q: Money supply grows 5 percent and velocity grows 1 percent. What is the implied growth rate of nominal GDP?
correctAnswer: Approximately 6 percent.
distractors: Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 5 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
commonError: Subtracting velocity growth from money growth when calculating nominal-spending growth.
feedback: Because MV equals nominal GDP, its growth is approximately money growth plus velocity growth: 5 + 1 = 6 percent.
options: Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 5 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 6 percent.

q: A student claims that faster money growth can permanently raise real output at the same rate. What is the best long-run correction?
correctAnswer: In the long run, sustained money growth mainly raises inflation, not real output.
distractors: Sustained money growth permanently raises real output but never prices.
Money growth has no effect on either nominal or real variables.
Velocity always adjusts to eliminate every effect of money growth.
commonError: Extending short-run output effects into a permanent long-run relationship.
feedback: In the long run, real output is determined mainly by real factors, so sustained excess money growth appears largely as inflation.
options: In the long run, sustained money growth mainly raises inflation, not real output.
Sustained money growth permanently raises real output but never prices.
Money growth has no effect on either nominal or real variables.
Velocity always adjusts to eliminate every effect of money growth.

q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?
correctAnswer: Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
distractors: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.
options: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.

q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
correctAnswer: Outside the labor force.
distractors: Unemployed.
Employed.
Frictionally employed.
commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.
options: Unemployed.
Employed.
Outside the labor force.
Frictionally employed.

q: Which equation defines the labor force?
correctAnswer: Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.
distractors: Labor force = population + unemployed people.
Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
commonError: Including everyone in the population or excluding officially unemployed workers.
feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.
options: Labor force = population + unemployed people.
Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.

q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?
correctAnswer: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
distractors: It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.
commonError: Assuming the unemployment rate can fall only when employment rises.
feedback: When a discouraged worker exits the labor force, both the number unemployed and the denominator fall, which can lower the rate.
options: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.

q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?
correctAnswer: The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
distractors: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.
commonError: Using the adult population as the unemployment-rate denominator or omitting unemployed workers from participation.
feedback: The labor force is 1,000, so unemployment is 100/1,000 = 10 percent; participation is 1,000/1,200 = 83.3 percent.
options: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.

q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?
correctAnswer: Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
distractors: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.
commonError: Treating job loss with active search as labor-force exit.
feedback: The person moves from employed to unemployed but remains in the labor force, raising the unemployment rate.
options: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.

q: A drought shifts the supply of staple food left, while a binding price ceiling remains fixed below the new equilibrium price. Which combined result is most likely?
correctAnswer: The shortage grows and nonprice rationing becomes more important.
distractors: The shortage disappears because the ceiling protects buyers.
Quantity supplied rises because the legal price is unchanged.
The market reaches the new equilibrium without any rationing.
commonError: Analyzing the supply shock without recognizing the binding price ceiling and hidden rationing costs.
feedback: The leftward supply shift widens the gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the controlled price.
options: The shortage disappears because the ceiling protects buyers.
Quantity supplied rises because the legal price is unchanged.
The market reaches the new equilibrium without any rationing.
The shortage grows and nonprice rationing becomes more important.

q: The government cuts taxes while the central bank raises interest rates. What is the strongest conclusion about aggregate demand?
correctAnswer: The net shift is uncertain because the policies oppose each other.
distractors: Aggregate demand must rise because tax cuts always dominate.
Aggregate demand must fall because interest rates always dominate.
Both policies reduce consumption and investment.
commonError: Declaring a definite aggregate-demand result without comparing opposing policy effects.
feedback: The tax cut supports consumption, while higher interest rates restrain investment and durable spending; relative magnitudes determine the net shift.
options: The net shift is uncertain because the policies oppose each other.
Aggregate demand must rise because tax cuts always dominate.
Aggregate demand must fall because interest rates always dominate.
Both policies reduce consumption and investment.

q: Nominal GDP rises 8 percent while the GDP deflator rises 5 percent. At the same time, unemployment falls. What is the best interpretation?
correctAnswer: Real output rose about 3 percent, prices increased, and the labor market strengthened.
distractors: Real output grew 13 percent because nominal and price growth should be added.
All nominal GDP growth was inflation, so real output was unchanged.
The unemployment decline proves the price level fell.
commonError: Treating nominal GDP growth as real growth or ignoring the price index.
feedback: A rough real-growth estimate subtracts inflation from nominal growth: 8 - 5 = 3 percent, consistent with improving employment conditions.
options: Real output grew 13 percent because nominal and price growth should be added.
Real output rose about 3 percent, prices increased, and the labor market strengthened.
All nominal GDP growth was inflation, so real output was unchanged.
The unemployment decline proves the price level fell.

q: Productivity improves and shifts long-run aggregate supply right while a separate fiscal expansion shifts aggregate demand right. What can be predicted with confidence?
correctAnswer: Real output rises, but the price-level effect is ambiguous.
distractors: The price level and real output both must rise.
The price level and real output both must fall.
Real output is unchanged because supply and demand shifts cancel.
commonError: Assuming two rightward shifts must move both equilibrium variables in the same direction.
feedback: Both shifts raise equilibrium output, but stronger supply lowers the price level while stronger demand raises it.
options: The price level and real output both must rise.
The price level and real output both must fall.
Real output rises, but the price-level effect is ambiguous.
Real output is unchanged because supply and demand shifts cancel.

q: A policy proposal claims it will “improve fairness” and also predicts that employment will rise. What should an analyst do first?
correctAnswer: Separate the fairness judgment from the testable employment prediction.
distractors: Treat both statements as positive because they concern policy.
Reject both statements because models cannot study policy.
Combine both statements into one numerical forecast.
commonError: Mixing a value judgment with a testable economic prediction.
feedback: Fairness is a normative criterion, while the employment effect is a positive claim that can be tested with evidence.
options: Treat both statements as positive because they concern policy.
Reject both statements because models cannot study policy.
Combine both statements into one numerical forecast.
Separate the fairness judgment from the testable employment prediction.

q: A worker receives a 4 percent nominal wage increase while consumer prices rise 6 percent. What bridge calculation is needed before judging living standards?
correctAnswer: Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
distractors: Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.
commonError: Evaluating purchasing power from nominal wages without adjusting for inflation.
feedback: Approximate real wage growth equals nominal wage growth minus inflation: 4 - 6 = -2 percent.
options: Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.
